analysis.one_liner: Requires pharmacy benefit managers to pay pharmacies fairly and bans spread pricing, steering, and clawback fees.
analysis.headline: Despite 55 cosponsors split almost evenly between the parties, the bill never received a committee vote before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set the rules for how pharmacy benefit managers — the middlemen insurers hire to run prescription drug plans — pay pharmacies under federal health programs like Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, and the federal employees' plan. It would force PBMs to pay pharmacies at the national average cost of a drug plus a set dispensing fee, and would ban practices like spread pricing (charging the program more than the pharmacy is paid), fees that claw back pharmacy reimbursement, and steering patients to PBM-owned pharmacies. It would also require that most manufacturer rebates be applied to lower patients' out-of-pocket costs at the pharmacy counter, backed by felony penalties and whistleblower lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with drug coverage under Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, or the federal employees' plan would see out-of-pocket costs calculated with most rebates passed through at the point of sale, and would keep access to any in-network pharmacy instead of being pushed to PBM-owned ones. Community and independent pharmacies would get guaranteed reimbursement at the national average drug cost plus a dispensing fee, and an end to post-adjudication fees that cut their pay after the fact.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal drug-plan patients and local pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Requires PBMs administering federal drug plans to reimburse in-network pharmacies at the national average drug acquisition cost plus a dispensing fee equal to the state's Medicaid dispensing fee [S2].

Bans spread pricing, steering patients to PBM-affiliate pharmacies, requiring brand-name drugs when cheaper generics exist, and any post-adjudication fees or adjustments that reduce pharmacy reimbursement [S2].
Requires patient cost sharing to be calculated at the pharmacy counter with at least 80% of manufacturer rebates deducted from the price [S2].
Imposes felony penalties of up to $1 million per violation and 10 years in prison for knowing violations, and allows whistleblower-style civil actions modeled on the False Claims Act [S2].

Broadens Medicaid's drug-price surveys to cover all pharmacy types — including mail-order and PBM-owned specialty pharmacies — and requires the government to publish national drug acquisition price data and report non-response rates [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The three dominant PBMs — CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, and Optum Rx — and the insurers that own them (CVS Health, Cigna, and UnitedHealth) would lose the spread pricing margins, clawback fees, and rebate-related revenue the bill outlaws, and would face steep penalties for violations. Federal programs and plan sponsors could see higher costs if pharmacies' guaranteed reimbursement exceeds what plans pay today.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their insurer owners

drawbacks.text: Guaranteeing every pharmacy the national average drug cost plus a dispensing fee, while banning outcome- or performance-based reimbursement adjustments, could raise drug-plan costs and federal program spending, which could show up as premiums or taxpayer costs [S2].

A one-size-fits-all reimbursement formula based on average acquisition cost may not cover pharmacies that buy at above-average prices, and eliminating performance metrics removes incentives tied to service quality [S2].
The felony penalty of up to $1 million per act and whistleblower lawsuits could invite aggressive litigation over billing disputes that are now handled by audits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections and pharmacy payment guarantees are substantial and target practices with well-documented costs to patients and independent pharmacies, but the fixed reimbursement formula and ban on all performance-based adjustments are blunt instruments that could raise plan costs without a spending offset. A well-designed version would trade some of that rigidity for accountability on quality.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, sat there through a December subcommittee referral, and never got a markup, a floor vote, or a Senate companion before Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) and Rep. Diana Harshbarger (R-TN) introduced the Pharmacists Fight Back Act on July 23, 2024 [S2].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Oversight, and Armed Services committees on the day of introduction [S4].
The bill drew 55 cosponsors, split 29 Republicans and 26 Democrats [S3].
On December 17, 2024, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health — the last recorded action [S4].
No markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The dominant pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that own them — CVS Health, Cigna, and UnitedHealth — kept the spread pricing margins, clawback fees, and rebate-driven revenue the bill would have outlawed, and community pharmacies kept absorbing post-adjudication fee cuts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their parent insurers

sides.party_line_note: The two original sponsors were one Democrat and one Republican, and cosponsorship split nearly evenly — 29 Republicans to 26 Democrats — so the bill died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill would outlaw the core of PBM profit on federal drug claims: spread pricing, post-adjudication clawback fees, steering patients to PBM-owned pharmacies, and keeping rebates out of patient cost sharing, with felony penalties attached. Their gain today comes directly out of what patients and pharmacies keep.

Pharmacies would get guaranteed reimbursement at the national average drug cost plus a state-set dispensing fee, and an end to fees that cut their pay after a claim is processed. Small pharmacies are the ones squeezed hardest by current PBM practices.

industries.industry: Insurers that own PBMs (UnitedHealth, CVS Health, Cigna)
industries.note: These vertically integrated companies would lose the PBM-side revenue the bill targets, though their insurance plans would also benefit from lower pharmacy reimbursement obligations. The bill would loosen, not break, their control of the drug supply chain.
